newsitem.title: USA: Simpson defense attacks slain ex-wife.
newsitem.headline: Simpson defense attacks slain ex-wife.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's defence attorney on Thursday attacked the character of the former football star's slain ex-wife, accusing her of partying with prostitutes and drug users and of having an abortion.
Nicole Brown's mother, Juditha, and her sister, Denise, left the courtroom in obvious distress mid-way through Robert Baker's opening statement at Simpson's civil trial.
It was the strongest sign yet that the defence team plans to present tawdry details of his ex-wife's private life in an effort to clear Simpson's name.

Listing a litany of events after Nicole Brown Simpson filed for divorce in February 1992, Baker said she threw parties at her Brentwood home to which she invited prostitutes and drug users and drank to excess.
He also alleged she had a series of lovers, ended an unwanted pregnancy with an abortion and was caught by Simpson having oral sex with one of her boyfriends.

Simpson was found not guilty by a criminal court jury in October last year of murdering his ex-wife and her friend, Ronald Goldman, on the night of June 12, 1994. He is being sued for wrongful death by the families of the victims and could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages if the jury finds him responsible for the deaths.

Baker told the jurors Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were dating and Goldman would have gone to Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium on the night of the murders whether or not he was delivering glasses left earlier by Nicole Brown Simpson's mother at the restaurant where he worked.
"Nicole Brown Simpson's best friend will say they had a date that night. Ronald Goldman was in fact going to Nicole Brown Simpson's condo that night," Baker said.

Baker, painting a vastly different picture of Nicole Brown Simpson than lawyers for the plaintiffs on Wednesday, told the jury: "O.J. had gone to Nicole's house one evening and walked up the front walkway -- this was in 1992 -- and looked into the front room and saw Nicole performing oral sex on (a man)."

Simpson's ex-wife, he added, was "having parties, inviting drug users into her house with his (Simpson's) children." One of the partygoers was her close friend, Faye Resnick, who was "heavily into drugs...," Baker said.

Referring to an incident in 1993 when Simpson kicked down the back door of his ex-wife's house, Baker said: "He was hot, there was no question about it. He did not want prostitutes and drug users in his house."
During this period, Baker said, Nicole Brown Simpson's "mood swings were enormous ... she was drinking to excess."
Despite this, Baker told the jury, Simpson remained friends with her. "O.J. Simpson became and was Nicole's confidant" after their divorce, he said.
Baker said that after filing for divorce, "Nicole was exercising her wings. She had many boyfriends. When she had boyfriend problems she went to O.J. Simpson.

"In the summer of '92 she became pregnant by one of her boyfriends and she turned to O.J. Simpson for moral support. She didn't tell her mother, she didn't tell the boyfriend, she turned to O.J. Simpson. She decided to terminate an apparently unwanted pregnancy. That's how much of a confidant he was."
Baker said Nicole Brown Simpson also turned to her ex-husband for help when she crashed her Ferrari car "in rather dubious circumstances."
He also said it was Nicole Brown Simpson who had pursued Simpson after the divorce, begging him to take her back, and not, as the jury had previously heard, the other way around.

Turning to the murders, Baker said at 9:30 p.m. on the night of the killings two men rollerblading past Nicole Brown Simpson's home saw a "Spanish or Caucasian" person hiding in the bushes outside the house. They contacted police who interviewed them twice but apparently did not follow up on the information, Baker said.
Laurie Levenson, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University and a former federal prosecutor, said attacking Nicole Brown Simpson's character could backfire.

"It's a risky approach. You create sympathy toward the victim and animosity toward (Simpson)," she said. She added that the "trashing of Nicole" was something that Simpson's attorneys in the criminal trial had studiously avoided.
